analysis.one_liner: Requires cities receiving federal community development grants to report on their zoning and land-use policies.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by senators from both parties, was referred to the Senate Banking Committee in May 2023 and never received a hearing, a vote, or further action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Cities that receive Community Development Block Grant money would have to file a plan with HUD describing, for a long list of land-use policies — allowing duplexes and apartment buildings in single-family zones, faster permitting, smaller minimum lot sizes, fewer parking mandates, and more — whether they have adopted each policy, plan to, or why it would benefit the community. The report would not be binding: a city could still keep its zoning exactly as it is, and HUD could not withhold grant money over the plan's content [S3]. The point is transparency: to surface and discourage exclusionary zoning that limits housing supply and raises costs [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: Renters and prospective homebuyers in cities with restrictive zoning, indirectly. The bill does not force any city to change its rules; it requires CDBG entitlement communities to file a plan describing their adoption, implementation plans, or the benefits of a list of pro-housing land-use policies, and its stated purpose is to 'discourage the use of discriminatory land use policies and remove barriers to making housing more affordable' [S3]. Making zoning restrictions visible to HUD and the public is aimed at easing the housing shortage that raises rents and prices [S2]. Developers and homebuilders would also benefit if cities subsequently adopt policies like by-right multifamily zoning and streamlined permitting, since these open more land to building [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Renters and buyers priced out by restrictive zoning

how_it_helps.text: Requires certain Community Development Block Grant recipients to submit a plan tracking whether they have adopted, plan to adopt, or would benefit from policies such as high-density zoning, allowing duplexes and fourplexes in single-family areas, reducing minimum lot sizes, cutting parking mandates, and streamlining permitting [S2][S3].
States the purpose is to discourage discriminatory land use policies and remove barriers to housing affordability, furthering the intent of the CDBG program [S3].
The submission is expressly not binding and cannot affect how a recipient uses or distributes its grant money, so the tool is transparency rather than coercion [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Local governments that receive CDBG entitlement grants, which would bear the administrative cost of preparing a standardized land-use report for HUD at least once every five years [S3]. Homeowners and local officials who benefit from restrictive zoning would face public disclosure of policies like single-family-only zoning and large minimum lot sizes, which the bill is designed to discourage [S3]. Federal taxpayers continue funding the CDBG program unchanged [S2].

drawbacks.text: The requirement is purely informational: a plan's submission 'shall not be binding with respect to the use or distribution of amounts' and acceptance 'is not an endorsement or approval,' so a city could describe its exclusionary zoning and change nothing — critics could fairly call the bill toothless [S3].
It adds an unfunded reporting obligation for local governments, which must prepare standardized plans for roughly two dozen policy categories before receiving grants each year [S3].

Many local officials view land use as a local matter; a federal mandate to report on zoning decisions — even a non-binding one — was likely to draw objections as federal intrusion into local zoning [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs are small — paperwork for grant-receiving cities — but so are the direct benefits, since nothing in the bill requires a city to change its zoning. The realistic value is informational: standardized disclosure of exclusionary land-use practices, which supporters hoped would pressure cities to legalize more housing over time. A well-designed version might have attached consequences or funding incentives to the reporting; this one relies on sunlight alone.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in May 2023, read twice, and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote until Congress ended in January 2025 [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Sen. Todd Young (R-IN), joined by Sen. Brian Schatz (D-HI), introduced the Yes In My Backyard Act on May 18, 2023 [S1][S3].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs — the only action it ever received [S5].
Seven senators cosponsored the bill, four Democrats and three Republicans [S4].
The committee never scheduled a hearing or markup, and the bill never reached the Senate floor before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Jurisdictions with restrictive zoning, which avoided the new federal reporting requirement, and the exclusionary-zoning status quo, which the bill was designed to surface but never got the chance to.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Restrictive-zoning status quo; no new reporting

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan from the start — Republican Sen. Young introduced it with Democratic Sen. Schatz, and the seven cosponsors split 4 Democrats and 3 Republicans [S4] — so the bill died from inaction rather than a party-line fight.

industries.note: By pressing cities toward by-right multifamily zoning, faster permitting, and smaller lots, the bill's list of policies would open more land to residential construction if adopted, expanding the market for builders [S3]. More housing supply is the mechanism by which renters and buyers would benefit too [S2].

industries.industry: Local governments receiving CDBG entitlement grants
industries.note: They would bear an unfunded obligation to prepare and submit standardized land-use plans to HUD at least once every five years before receiving grants [S3]. The requirement is reporting only and cannot affect their grant money, so the cost is administrative [S3].

industries.industry: Owners and communities protected by exclusionary zoning
industries.note: Single-family-only zoning and large minimum lots restrict supply and support property values for existing owners; the bill forces disclosure of such policies and states a purpose of discouraging them, though it cannot compel change [S3].
